title: Five Minutes Before Fajr
script: Narrator: [warmly] My grandfather kept a small alarm clock beside his bed. It rang a few minutes before his usual alarm for Fajr.
Narrator: At first, I thought he needed extra time to wake up. Then I stayed at his house and learned the real reason.
Narrator: [quietly] When the first alarm rang, he sat up and made a short dua. He asked Allah to help someone by name.
Narrator: The person changed from week to week. Sometimes it was a sick relative, a neighbor with debt, or a student taking an exam.
Narrator: [carefully] He never told those people about these private prayers. He did not send a message saying, “I prayed for you.”
Narrator: After the dua, he prepared for salah. The whole habit took only a few quiet minutes.
Narrator: [curious] I asked how he remembered so many needs. He showed me a folded paper inside a drawer.
Narrator: The paper contained names and brief notes. He updated it when someone recovered or when a new need appeared.
Narrator: [practically] My grandfather said practical help was also important. He visited, shared food, and gave money when he could.
Narrator: [thoughtful] But there were problems he could not solve with his own hands. Dua kept him connected to people without pretending to control their results.
Narrator: I liked that the habit was hidden. It did not build an image of him as a caring person; it simply trained him to care.
Narrator: [inspired] After returning home, I made a small list of my own. I began with three names and one community need.
Narrator: Some mornings I forget, so I keep the paper near my alarm. The goal is not a perfect record.
Narrator: [reflective] Those five minutes teach me that another person's struggle should not disappear from my heart when the conversation ends.
Narrator: A quiet dua costs nothing, but it can live beside real service and sincere concern.
